To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of low cost, mobile chemical sensors can help to develop data literacy among students and the general public.

(1) the project has successfully engaged students from a range of disciplines and from a range of educational levels in the process of developing and testing low-cost chemical sensors for environmental monitoring, (2) the project has engaged a range of stakeholders in the process of identifying and collecting representative test data sets, (3) the project has developed a range of tools to visualize the data collected, (4) the project has begun to educate the public on the effect of priority contaminants on human and environmental heath,

(1) the use of low-cost chemical sensors in citizen science is a powerful tool to build capacity for understanding and analyzing the chemical footprint of human activities on our planet and to develop the capacity of young people to make decisions based on chemical measurement data; and (2) that international collaboration is a key element for building capacity to understand and analyze complex chemical data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new type of chemical data literacy that is based on the use of simple, low cost, portable sensors for environmental monitoring.

the development of a new type of chemical literacy that is based on a data-driven approach to the understanding of the chemical environment and the development of data analysis skills that are needed to make sense of the information.

the development of a new type of data literate citizen scientist who can understand, interpret and act upon the chemical data collected from the environment using simple, inexpensive, mobile chemical sensors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the project is a success, but it is still in the process of becoming one.
the OPCW has developed a project with a strong educational component that will build capacity in young people for responsible chemical analysis.
the OPCW is committed to building capacity for responsible science that is locally relevant, and that this project is an effort to do that.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the project is a success in that it has brought together an international group of students and faculty to work collaboratively on a project that has relevance to their local contexts and that is based on the development and application of low cost chemical sensors.

we have developed an approach to building capacity for responsible science through the development of low-cost chemical sensor technology and data analysis and visualization tools that can be applied in a variety of contexts.
we have built a network of students and faculty from 14 institutions in 8 countries, and we have developed the capacity for international collaboration on chemical analysis and data collection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is feasible for students, teachers and citizen scientists to build their own chemical sensors for environmental analysis, collect data on priority contaminants and use that data to make decisions about chemical exposure and risk.

it is possible for young people around the globe to use simple chemical sensors to measure chemical pollutants and that this is an excellent way to build data literacy in the context of the global chemical footprint.
it is possible to build a global network of citizen science and international collaboration for environmental monitoring with simple sensors.
